title: Averages & Basic Statistics
coreInsight: The mean is the equal-share or balance value determined by a total, while median, mode, and range describe different features of a data set.
targetLearnerRealization: The mean is the level obtained by preserving the total while redistributing it equally.
learningObjectives: Interpret the mean as an equal-share value that preserves the total.
Use total = mean × count to combine groups and recover missing values.
Distinguish mean, median, mode, and range.
Weight subgroup means by their group sizes.

continuity.openingCallback: Use equal parts and division to rebalance unequal piles without changing their total.
closingSeeds: A numerical summary compresses a data set but can hide its shape.
A visual display can reveal clusters, gaps, and trends that a single average cannot.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: The mean must be one of the observed data values.
Average always means the middle value.
Averages of groups can be averaged without considering group sizes.
The mean can be manipulated without tracking the underlying total.

beats.purpose: Create the mean by redistributing four unequal piles while preserving their total.
beats.expectedRealization: The balanced height is total divided by number of piles.
beats.transitionIn: Equal parts named fractions. Now redistribute unequal piles into equal shares without creating or losing any counters.
beats.prompt: Four piles contain 2, 4, 6, and 8 counters. If all 20 counters are shared equally among the four piles, how many counters will each pile contain?

visual.ariaLabel: Four bars containing two, four, six, and eight units

response.feedback: Preserve the total of 20 while making four equal shares.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Twenty counters shared across four piles gives five per pile.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add the pile sizes first, then divide by the number of piles.

visual.ariaLabel: Four equal bars each containing five units

steps.title: Preserve the total
steps.body: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20 counters. Moving counters between piles does not change 20.

resolution.takeaway: The mean is the equal-share level that preserves the total.

beats.purpose: Show that the equal-share mean need not be an observed data value or a whole number.
beats.expectedRealization: A mean describes a balance point, not necessarily an existing observation.
beats.transitionIn: The balanced height happened to be a whole number. Change the total so equal sharing lands between whole numbers.
beats.prompt: Three piles contain 2, 3, and 6 liters. What is their mean amount?

options.text: 3 liters, because 3 is the middle observation.
3 2/3 liters, because 11 liters are shared among 3 piles.
6 liters, because it is the largest observation.
11 liters, because that is the total.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The equal share is 11/3 = 3 2/3 liters, even though no original pile has that amount.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add all three amounts and divide the total by three piles.

steps.body: 2 + 3 + 6 = 11 liters, and 11 ÷ 3 = 3 2/3 liters. The mean is a balance value, so it need not appear in the data.

resolution.takeaway: A mean can lie between observed values.

beats.purpose: Contrast mean, median, mode, and range on one small data set.
beats.expectedRealization: Different statistics answer different questions about the same data.
beats.transitionIn: Equal sharing describes one feature. Keep the data fixed and ask three different questions.
beats.prompt: For the ordered data 1, 2, 2, 9, which row correctly gives mean, median, mode, and range?

options.text: mean 3.5, median 2, mode 2, range 8
mean 2, median 3.5, mode 9, range 8
mean 3.5, median 2, mode 1, range 9
mean 14, median 2, mode 2, range 10

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Each statistic captures a different feature of the same four numbers.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute equal share, average the two middle positions, find the repeated value, and subtract minimum from maximum.

steps.title: Mean
steps.body: The total is 14, so the mean is 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5.

steps.title: Median and mode
steps.body: The middle values are 2 and 2, so the median is 2; the repeated value 2 is also the mode.

steps.title: Range
steps.body: The spread from minimum to maximum is 9 − 1 = 8.

resolution.takeaway: Mean balances, median locates the middle, mode tracks frequency, and range measures span.

beats.purpose: Name the four summary statistics after their meanings have been contrasted.
beats.expectedRealization: Average is ambiguous unless the intended statistic is specified.
beats.transitionIn: The word “average” can hide several distinct summaries, so name the one you mean.
beats.name: Mean, median, mode, and range
beats.conciseDefinition: The mean is total divided by count; the median is the middle ordered value; the mode is most frequent; the range is maximum minus minimum.

beats.purpose: Apply total preservation to percentages from differently sized groups.
beats.expectedRealization: Each percentage must be converted back to a correct-count total before the tests combine.
beats.transitionIn: A mean hides a total. These test percentages also hide totals, and the tests do not contain equal numbers of questions.
beats.whyNow: The learner knows total = mean × count; differently sized tests expose why subgroup percentages cannot be averaged naively.
beats.entryBridge: Recover the number correct on each test before combining anything.
beats.exitBridge: Fifty correct answers out of sixty questions determine the combined percentage.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Quantity bars whose filled totals are merged before rebalancing.
learnerPrompts: At the first step, notice that the three percentage bars represent 10, 20, and 30 questions.
When correct counts appear, compute 70% of 10, 80% of 20, and 90% of 30.
At the combined bar, add correct answers and total questions separately.
At the final step, convert 50/60 to the nearest offered percent.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The combined score is 50 out of 60, about 83%.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Do not average 70, 80, and 90 equally; the tests contain different numbers of questions.

steps.title: Convert
steps.body: 50/60 ≈ 83.3%, so the closest answer is D, 83%.

resolution.takeaway: Weight each subgroup by its size by recovering its total contribution.

beats.purpose: Directly diagnose naive averaging of two subgroup means.
beats.expectedRealization: A larger group contributes more to the combined mean.
beats.transitionIn: The three tests exposed hidden group sizes. Test the same idea with two class sections.
beats.prompt: A 10-student group has mean score 80. A 30-student group has mean score 90. What is the combined mean?

options.text: 85, by averaging the two displayed means equally.
87.5, after combining score totals for all 40 students.
90, because the larger group replaces the smaller.
170, by adding the means.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The 30-student group contributes three times as many scores, pulling the combined mean toward 90.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Convert each mean back to a total score using mean × count, then combine all 40 students.

steps.title: Rebalance everyone
steps.body: The total is 3,500 across 40 students, so 3,500 ÷ 40 = 87.5.

resolution.takeaway: Subgroup means need weights equal to their group sizes.

beats.purpose: Connect mean's total-preservation habit to a distinct equal-sum structure without claiming it is an average problem.
beats.expectedRealization: Tracking how often each value is counted can recover a hidden total relationship.
beats.transitionIn: Equal sharing is one use of total preservation. In this cross, the challenge is different: the center is counted in both equal sums.
beats.whyNow: The approved puzzle broadens the total-tracking habit: learners must account for a duplicated center before optimizing the common sum.
beats.entryBridge: Add the horizontal and vertical sums and track which tile is counted twice.
beats.exitBridge: A correct total account turns a spatial puzzle into one equation and a pairing check.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A fixed total redistributed into equal-sum structures.
learnerPrompts: At the first step, identify the one square counted in both sums.
When 2S = 35 + c appears, explain the extra center term.
At the candidate step, choose the largest center that still permits equal outside pairs.
At the final cross, verify both arm sums directly.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Centering 13 permits outside pairs summing to 11, so each full arm sums to 24.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The five tiles total 35, but adding both arm sums counts the center twice.

steps.title: Track the duplicated center
steps.body: If each arm sums to S and the center is c, then 2S = 35 + c.

steps.title: Check the arrangement
steps.body: The remaining values pair as 1 + 10 = 11 and 4 + 7 = 11. Adding center 13 makes both arms 24, so the answer is D.

resolution.takeaway: Preserve totals—and count repeated contributions exactly.

beats.purpose: Consolidate total-based mean reasoning and distinguish the four summaries.
beats.expectedRealization: The statistic and group structure determine what must be preserved or counted.
beats.transitionIn: Piles, tests, class groups, and the cross all rewarded careful accounting of totals.

options.text: A mean and a count determine the underlying total.
The mean must be one of the observed values.
Combining group means requires their group sizes.
Median, mode, and range describe features different from equal share.
Average always means the middle ordered value.

response.feedback: Separate equal sharing from position, frequency, and spread, and keep totals attached to group sizes.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. The mean preserves total; the other summaries answer different questions.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Discard claims that force the mean to be observed or confuse it with the median.

steps.title: Mean
steps.body: Use total = mean × count and mean = total ÷ count.

steps.title: Groups
steps.body: Recover each group's total before merging unequal group sizes.

steps.title: Other summaries
steps.body: Median uses order, mode uses frequency, and range uses the endpoints.

resolution.takeaway: Choose the summary by the feature you need.

beats.purpose: Create the successor need for visual data representation after numerical summaries.
beats.expectedRealization: A single summary can hide patterns in the individual values.
beats.transitionIn: A mean compresses a list to one balance value. Compression can hide the list's shape.
beats.prompt: Two data sets can share the same mean and range but arrange their values differently. What would help reveal clusters, gaps, or trends?

options.text: A graph or table showing the individual values.
Only the mean, repeated twice.
Deleting the units and labels.
Sorting the statistic names alphabetically.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. A visual display can preserve the individual values while exposing their pattern.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Choose a representation that keeps more of the data visible than one summary number.

steps.body: Tables organize exact values; graphs use position, length, or height to make comparisons and patterns visible. The next question is how to choose and read those displays without letting their scales mislead us.

resolution.takeaway: A summary tells one feature; a display can reveal the data's shape.

notes: The generated pile model establishes equal-share meaning before terminology.
The weighted-test bank problem directly repairs naive averaging; the equal-cross bank problem is framed only as a total-preservation connection.
The lesson remains draft pending human pedagogical review.
